intro: Rugby league split from rugby union in 1895 and evolved into a faster, more structured game. Thirteen players a side have six tackles to move the ball upfield and score; after the sixth, possession passes to the opponents. Contested rucks are replaced by the quick 'play-the-ball', which keeps the game flowing. The International Rugby League (IRL) governs the sport worldwide.
inThirtySeconds: Score a try (4 points) by grounding the ball over the opponents' try line.
Each team gets six tackles per possession, usually kicking on the last one.
After a tackle, the player gets up and rolls the ball back with the foot — the play-the-ball.
Like union, passes must go backwards.
objective: Outscore the opponent with tries, conversions, penalty goals and drop goals over 80 minutes.

facts.environment: Grass or artificial pitch with H-shaped posts

scoring.label: Try
scoring.detail: Grounding the ball on or over the opponents' try line.

scoring.label: Conversion
scoring.detail: Kick at goal after a try.

scoring.label: Penalty goal
scoring.detail: Kick at goal awarded after an infringement.

scoring.label: Drop goal
scoring.detail: A drop kick over the crossbar in open play (also called a field goal).

bodies.name: International Rugby League
bodies.scope: World governing body for rugby league

rulebooks.title: International Rugby League Laws of the Game

chapters.title: Six tackles
chapters.summary: Possession is rationed — use it well.

rules.title: The six-tackle set
rules.summary: A team in possession may be tackled five times; on the sixth tackle, the ball is handed over to the opponents.
rules.body: Because of this, teams usually run the ball for five tackles and kick on the last ('last-tackle option') to gain territory or chase a try. If the defending team touches the ball in certain ways, or gives away an infringement, the attacking team may get a fresh set of six.
rules.example: On tackle five a halfback kicks high towards the corner, hoping a winger can catch it and score before the defenders.

rules.title: The play-the-ball
rules.summary: After being tackled, the player stands up, places the ball on the ground and rolls it backwards with the foot to a teammate.
rules.body: One or two defenders ('markers') may stand directly opposite; the rest of the defence must retreat a set distance (usually 10 m) until the ball is played. This is what makes rugby league fast and continuous.

rules.title: Backward passes only
rules.summary: Passes must not travel forward; a forward pass or knock-on usually results in a scrum to the opponents.
rules.body: Scrums in rugby league are a restart rather than a contest of strength, and some competitions replace them with a simple handover in certain situations.

rules.title: Offside at the play-the-ball
rules.summary: Defenders must retreat the required distance and may not move up before the ball is played.
rules.body: Being offside, interfering with the play-the-ball, or holding a tackled player down too long gives the attacking team a penalty — and often a new set of six.

rules.title: 40/20 and kicking for touch
rules.summary: A kick from inside your own half that bounces into touch inside the opponents' 20 m area earns a reward, under current international laws and major leagues.
rules.body: This '40/20' kick rewards accurate tactical kicking. Exact rules (whether you win the feed at a scrum or restart with a tap) vary between competitions, so check the competition's current laws.

rules.title: Penalties
rules.summary: For a penalty, the team can kick for goal (2 points), kick for touch, or tap and run.
rules.body: Kicking for touch gives the team the restart near where the ball went out and a fresh set of tackles.

rules.title: Sin bin and send-offs
rules.summary: Foul play can earn a 10-minute sin bin or a send-off for the rest of the match.
rules.body: High tackles, shoulder charges and dangerous throws are common reasons. Competitions also review incidents afterwards and can suspend players.

fouls.name: Knock-on / forward pass
fouls.description: The ball goes forward from the hands.

fouls.name: Offside
fouls.description: Defender not back the required distance at the play-the-ball.

fouls.name: Holding down
fouls.description: Slowing the tackled player from getting up.

fouls.name: High tackle
fouls.description: Contact with the head or neck.

flow.title: Kick-off
flow.description: Each half begins with a place kick from halfway.

flow.title: Sets of six
flow.description: Teams take turns attacking in sets of six tackles.

flow.title: Last-tackle kicks
flow.description: Kicks to gain territory or force a goal-line drop-out.

flow.title: Full-time
flow.description: In some competitions, tied games go to golden-point extra time.

positions.name: Wings and centres (2–5)
positions.role: Outside backs who finish attacks and defend the edges.

positions.name: Props (8, 10)
positions.role: Big forwards who carry hard up the middle.

positions.name: Hooker (9)
positions.role: Distributes from the play-the-ball, like a dummy-half.

positions.name: Second row and loose forward (11–13)
positions.role: Mobile forwards who tackle and run edge lines.

field.name: Pitch
field.dimensions: 100 m between try lines × about 68 m wide, plus in-goal areas
notes: Lines every 10 m across the field

glossary.definition: The player who picks up the ball from the play-the-ball.
A team's run of six tackles.
Extra time in which the first score wins.
A restart kick from the goal line or the 20 m line.

funFacts: The 1895 split was largely about money: northern English clubs wanted to compensate working players for lost wages.
State of Origin, played between Queensland and New South Wales, is one of Australia's biggest sporting events.
